prompt: Three thousand people keep an event page open, and the page polls every three seconds. How many requests a second does boxoffice receive from them?
A dozen staff look at a sales dashboard that refreshes every minute. Which technique does the lesson say fits it?
hint: Few people, news that is not urgent.

choices.text: A WebSocket, because the dashboard is a live screen
choices.why: A WebSocket earns its machinery when the client talks back constantly; this one only reads.

choices.text: Centrifugo, so that deploys do not drop the dashboard
choices.why: A second server for twelve readers is the opposite of the lesson's advice.

choices.text: Long polling, since plain polling wastes the server
choices.why: Twelve requests a minute waste nothing worth a held request per viewer.

choices.text: Polling
choices.why: Right. A dozen requests a minute cost nothing, and there is no connection to keep alive.

prompt: Match each technique to how it works.

pairs.right: the page asks again every few seconds
the server holds the request until something changes
one GET whose response never ends
an HTTP request that turns into a two-way channel

prompt: Why does the lesson pick server-sent events, and not a WebSocket, as enough for seat availability?

choices.text: Browsers limit WebSockets to six per site
choices.why: The six-connection limit is HTTP/1.1's, and it hits server-sent event streams, not WebSockets.

choices.text: Server-sent events carry binary data, which a seat count needs
choices.why: Server-sent events are text only, and a count is a short text.

choices.text: The news flows one way, from server to viewer
choices.why: Right. The viewer never sends anything, so a two-way channel buys nothing.

choices.text: Go has no WebSocket support at all
choices.why: Section 05 builds one with coder/websocket.

prompt: A purchase runs the `UPDATE` on `sold`, then its transaction rolls back. What does a `LISTEN availability` session receive?

choices.text: A notification with the number from before the update
choices.why: Nothing is sent for that transaction at all.

choices.text: The notification, followed by a second one undoing it
choices.why: PostgreSQL sends no correction; the first one never left.

choices.text: The notification, sent the moment the trigger ran
choices.why: pg_notify queues the message; delivery waits for the commit.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Notifications are delivered at commit, and a rollback discards them.

prompt: The hub drops a value when a watcher's channel is full. Why is that safe for boxoffice?

choices.text: PostgreSQL sends every notification twice
choices.why: Each notification is delivered once to each listening session.

choices.text: Dropped values are written to the log and resent by the hub later
choices.why: The `default` branch does nothing; nothing is resent.

choices.text: The next message replaces the missed one
choices.why: Right. A missed value is corrected by the next sale's message.

choices.text: A full channel means the browser has closed
choices.why: A full channel means a slow reader; a closed one unsubscribes.

prompt: Why does `publish` offer each value with a `select` and a `default`, instead of a plain send?
hint: It holds the lock while it sends.

choices.text: A plain send on a buffered channel inside a loop over a map does not compile
choices.why: It compiles; it blocks when the buffer is full.

choices.text: `select` sends to all channels at once
choices.why: Each `select` here offers one value to one channel.

choices.text: PostgreSQL requires an answer before the next notification
choices.why: Notifications need no answer.

choices.text: One slow watcher would stall all the others
choices.why: Right. A blocked send under the mutex stalls the relay for everybody.

prompt: boxoffice's pool has `MaxConns` 10. How many connections are left for queries once `listen` is running?
hint: `listen` acquires one and never releases it.

prompt: Why does the migration wrap the function in `-- +goose StatementBegin` and `-- +goose StatementEnd`?
hint: Count the semicolons in the function body.

choices.text: They make the function run inside a transaction of its own
choices.why: goose already runs each migration in a transaction; the marks are about splitting.

choices.text: PostgreSQL rejects a plpgsql function body without them
choices.why: They are SQL comments; PostgreSQL never sees them as anything else.

choices.text: goose cuts statements at semicolons
choices.why: Right. Between the marks it sends everything as one statement.

choices.text: They mark the part `Down` undoes
choices.why: `-- +goose Down` marks that.

prompt: A `NOTIFY` payload has to stay under ___ bytes, which is why boxoffice sends an id and a number.
`liveEvents` subscribes to the hub before it reads the event from the store. What goes wrong in the other order?
hint: Picture a sale between the two steps.

choices.text: The store refuses reads from a handler that has no subscription in the hub yet
choices.why: The store knows nothing about the hub.

choices.text: The first message is sent twice
choices.why: Duplicates are what the chosen order risks, and they are harmless.

choices.text: The handler deadlocks on the hub's mutex
choices.why: Neither order holds the mutex across the read.

choices.text: A sale between them is missed until the next sale
choices.why: Right. Subscribing first at worst delivers the same number twice.

prompt: What would happen to the stream at ten seconds without `rc.SetWriteDeadline(time.Time{})`?

choices.text: Nothing; deadlines only apply to request bodies
choices.why: `WriteTimeout` applies to writing the response.

choices.text: `EventSource` would refuse a stream older than ten seconds
choices.why: The browser sets no such limit; the server's `WriteTimeout` does.

choices.text: `WriteTimeout` would cut the connection
choices.why: Right. The zero time lifts the deadline for this response only.

choices.text: The hub would unsubscribe the handler
choices.why: The hub has no clock.

prompt: The handler holds lesson 2's `statusRecorder`, not the connection's writer. How does `http.ResponseController` still flush?
hint: A method lesson 2 added for this lesson.

choices.text: `statusRecorder` implements `Flush` itself
choices.why: It declares only `WriteHeader`, `Write` and `Unwrap`; the wrapper hides `Flush`.

choices.text: It calls `Unwrap` to reach the writer underneath
choices.why: Right. `Unwrap` is the convention it follows through wrappers.

choices.text: It opens a second connection to the client
choices.why: A server never opens connections to a browser.

choices.text: Flushing happens anyway when the handler returns
choices.why: This handler returns only when the visitor leaves.

prompt: Put what `liveEvents` does in order.
items: subscribe to the event's availability in the hub
read the event from the store
lift the write deadline and set `text/event-stream`
write and flush the current availability
write each new value until the request's context ends

prompt: What ends one message in a `text/event-stream` response?

choices.text: A closing `}`
choices.why: The format is lines, not JSON.

choices.text: The end of the HTTP response
choices.why: The response never ends; messages need their own end.

choices.text: An empty line after the `data:` line
choices.why: Right. The handler writes `data: %d` followed by two newlines.

choices.text: A `Content-Length` header per message
choices.why: Headers are sent once, before the first message.

prompt: A page on `https://elsewhere.example.net` opens a WebSocket to boxoffice. Why does boxoffice's CORS middleware not protect it?

choices.text: The middleware runs after the upgrade
choices.why: Order is not the reason; CORS rules do not cover WebSockets.

choices.text: CORS governs `fetch`, and browsers apply no same-origin rule to WebSockets
choices.why: Right. So the server checks `Origin` itself, in `Accept`.

choices.text: WebSockets never send an `Origin` header
choices.why: Browsers send one on every WebSocket handshake.

choices.text: CORS only protects `POST`
choices.why: CORS covers every method a `fetch` sends.

prompt: The handshake from `curl` carried no `Origin` header at all. What did `Accept` answer?

choices.text: 403, because every request needs an Origin
choices.why: A request with no Origin passes; only browsers send one.

choices.text: 400, because the key was not random
choices.why: The RFC's sample key is a valid key.

choices.text: 101 Switching Protocols
choices.why: Right. Programs send no Origin and are not where this attack comes from.

choices.text: 200 with the availability as JSON
choices.why: A successful upgrade answers 101, and the data comes as frames.

prompt: boxoffice expects no messages from the client. Why does `liveSocket` still call `CloseRead`?
hint: Close and ping arrive as frames.

choices.text: `wsjson.Write` refuses to write until something was read
choices.why: Writing does not depend on reading.

choices.text: Without reading, close and ping frames go unanswered
choices.why: Right. CloseRead reads them in its own goroutine and ends the context on close.

choices.text: It lifts the write deadline
choices.why: Deadlines were already cleared by the hijack.

choices.text: It sends the first availability
choices.why: `send` does that.

prompt: Why does `liveSocket` need no `SetWriteDeadline`, unlike `liveEvents`?

choices.text: WebSocket connections last less than ten seconds
choices.why: They last as long as the client stays.

choices.text: `routes.go` serves `/ws` on a server with no timeouts
choices.why: Both routes share the one `http.Server` with its timeouts.

choices.text: The hijack clears the connection's deadlines
choices.why: Right. From then on deadlines are the WebSocket's own business.

choices.text: coder/websocket sets an infinite deadline before every write
choices.why: The handler gives every write five seconds instead.

prompt: A server that agrees to a WebSocket handshake answers with HTTP status ___.
Why does every write in `liveSocket` get a five-second timeout?

choices.text: Browsers drop frames older than five seconds
choices.why: Browsers keep every frame they receive.

choices.text: The RFC limits a frame to five seconds
choices.why: RFC 6455 sets no such limit.

choices.text: It spaces messages out so that the client keeps up with them
choices.why: A timeout caps a write; it never delays one.

choices.text: A full buffer would block it for good
choices.why: Right. The write fails, the handler returns, and the deferred cleanup runs.

prompt: Two clients are in the room and the second sends `doors open at 19:00`. Who receives it?

choices.text: Only the first client
choices.why: That is `BroadcastOthers`; the room uses `Broadcast`.

choices.text: Nobody until a third client joins
choices.why: Both transcripts show the message.

choices.text: Both clients, the sender included
choices.why: Right. `Broadcast` sends to every session.

choices.text: Only the server's log
choices.why: The log records joins and leaves, not messages.

prompt: Match each Melody default to its value.
What does `melody.New` do about the `Origin` of a handshake, and what does the lesson do about it?

choices.text: It accepts only the server's own host, like coder/websocket
choices.why: Melody's default is the opposite.

choices.text: It rejects every browser
choices.why: Any site's page joins the room.

choices.text: It accepts all; set `CheckOrigin` yourself
choices.why: Right. Its `CheckOrigin` returns true for everything.

choices.text: It reads the allowed origins from `config.go`
choices.why: `config.go` holds buffer and timing settings, not origins.

prompt: Why does the lesson run `sha256sum -c` before unpacking Centrifugo?
hint: It is the step people skip.

choices.text: `tar` refuses to unpack an archive that has no verified checksum beside it
choices.why: `tar` checks nothing of the kind.

choices.text: To pick the binary for the right platform
choices.why: The file name already picks the platform.

choices.text: To learn which Go version built it
choices.why: `centrifugo version` prints that.

choices.text: To check the download is the published file
choices.why: Right. The checksums file is published beside the archives.

prompt: Match each key of Centrifugo's `config.json` to what it is for.

pairs.right: signs the tokens clients connect with
the password a program publishes with
the sites whose pages are let in
the address and port it listens on

prompt: The log says `"engine":"memory"`. What happens if a second node with the same engine is added?

choices.text: The nodes share subscribers automatically
choices.why: Sharing them is what the Redis engine is for.

choices.text: It knows nothing about the first node's subscribers
choices.why: Right. The Redis engine is what lets several nodes share them.

choices.text: It refuses to start
choices.why: It starts; it just knows nothing of the first node's subscribers.

choices.text: Both nodes deliver every message twice
choices.why: Each node delivers only to its own subscribers.

prompt: The `connect` reply carried `"ping":25`. Every how many seconds does Centrifugo ping the connection?
Two copies of boxoffice run behind a load balancer. A viewer is on copy A and the sale happens on copy B. How does the viewer learn of it?

choices.text: PostgreSQL notifies both copies, and A's hub tells its own viewer
choices.why: Right. Taking the news from the database is what makes this work.

choices.text: Copy B forwards the sale to copy A over HTTP
choices.why: No copy talks to another.

choices.text: The viewer does not learn of it until reconnecting to B
choices.why: That is what a hub fed by `Sell` would do.

choices.text: The load balancer copies the stream to both copies
choices.why: A load balancer sends each connection to one copy.

prompt: A copy's listening connection was down for ten seconds. What happens to the notifications sent in that time?

choices.text: PostgreSQL resends them when the copy runs `LISTEN` again
choices.why: Nothing resends them; that copy never sees them.

choices.text: They wait in the hub's buffer
choices.why: The hub only receives what `listen` hands it.

choices.text: Lost; the next sale corrects that copy
choices.why: Right. Each message carries the whole number, so the next one corrects every screen.

choices.text: The transactions that sent them fail at commit
choices.why: Commits succeed whether anybody listens or not.

prompt: A proxy closes connections that send nothing for sixty seconds. What does the lesson propose for `liveEvents`?

choices.text: Raise `WriteTimeout` to an hour
choices.why: The deadline is already lifted; the proxy's idle timeout is the problem.

choices.text: A ticker that writes `: ping` every thirty seconds
choices.why: Right. Lines starting with a colon are comments to `EventSource`.

choices.text: Send the availability again every second
choices.why: That is polling with extra steps; a comment line costs less.

choices.text: Switch the route to long polling
choices.why: A held request meets the same idle timeout.

prompt: Why should clients reconnect after a deploy with a random delay?
hint: Every connection on the stopped process closes at once.

choices.text: Because `EventSource` refuses to reconnect at once
choices.why: It reconnects by itself a few seconds later.

choices.text: To hide the deploy from the access log
choices.why: The log records every request regardless.

choices.text: So ten thousand do not arrive in the same second
choices.why: Right. The delay spreads the reconnections out.

choices.text: So the database runs `LISTEN` first
choices.why: Clients do not affect the server's `LISTEN`.

prompt: Which statements about this lesson's design are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Dropping a value is right for a seat count and wrong for chat messages
choices.why: Right. A dropped number is replaced; a dropped sentence is lost.

choices.text: The trigger makes every way of changing `sold` announce itself
choices.why: Right. Even a manual `UPDATE` in psql fires it.

choices.text: Each hub channel holds every value until the browser reads it
choices.why: Each holds eight, and a ninth is dropped.

choices.text: `listen` returns its connection to the pool after each notification
choices.why: It keeps it for good, because `LISTEN` belongs to the session.

prompt: Order the path of one sale until a page shows the new number.
items: the transaction commits and the notification is delivered
`listen` hands the number to the hub
the handler writes it to the page

prompt: A team wants live seat counts for twenty thousand viewers, and deploys several times a day. Which choice matches the lesson's advice?

choices.text: Centrifugo, fed by `listen` through its publish API
choices.why: Right. Connections leave boxoffice, and the database stays the source of news.

choices.text: Melody, since its 256-message buffer handles the load
choices.why: Melody's connections live in the process, so a deploy still drops them.

choices.text: Polling every second from every viewer
choices.why: That is twenty thousand requests a second.

choices.text: A bigger hub buffer in boxoffice
choices.why: A buffer does nothing for connections dropped by a deploy.
